theme: Drought and sword; the deceitful heart; the Sabbath
readingInstruction: Read Jeremiah 14:1-17:27. A drought and a sword fall on Judah, Jeremiah refuses to marry or celebrate, and God exposes the human heart. Read 17:5-10 slowly, which contrasts the person who trusts in man with the one who trusts in the LORD.
settingTheScene: These chapters begin with a drought and a series of dialogues between Jeremiah and God. God tells him three times not to intercede for the people. The prophet’s personal life becomes part of the message: he is not to marry, mourn, or feast. Chapter 17 contains the famous passage on the deceitful heart, the blessed man, and a call to keep the Sabbath.
observation: “Though our iniquities testify against us, act, O LORD, for your name’s sake” (14:7).
“Then the LORD said to me, Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my heart would not turn toward this people” (15:1).
“Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart” (15:16).
“Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable?” (15:18).
“If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me” (15:19).
“Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the LORD” (17:5).
“Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, whose trust is the LORD” (17:7).
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?” (17:9).
interpretation:
The drought is a covenant curse. The land is parched, the cisterns are empty, the deer abandon their fawns. The people pray, but God says they love to wander. Even if Moses and Samuel interceded, he would not turn. The time for the warning is past. It is a hard thing for a prophet who loves his people. In chapter 15, Jeremiah is deeply wounded. His one consolation was God’s word: “Your words were found, and I ate them.” He consumed the word like food, and it was joy. But his joy led to isolation: he sat alone because God’s hand was on him. His complaint about God’s apparent unreliability, “like a deceitful brook,” draws a sharp reply: “If you return, I will restore you.” Even the prophet needs to repent.

Chapter 16 forbids Jeremiah to marry, mourn, or feast. His loneliness is a sermon: life as they know it is ending. And yet, in the middle, a promise that the people will be brought back from the north, and that a new exodus will eclipse the old one.

Chapter 17 is the heart of this section. The sin of Judah is written with an iron pen, engraved on the tablet of their heart. Then a pair of contrasting trees. The person who trusts in man is like a shrub in the desert, unaware of when good comes. The one who trusts in the LORD is like a tree planted by water, unafraid in the heat, still bearing fruit in drought. And the reason: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick.” No one can fully know his own heart. But the LORD searches it. This is why we need a new heart, not just better habits.
connection: Jesus said, “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John 15:5), and drew on the picture of fruitfulness. Psalm 1:3 describes the same tree. Mark 7:21-23 says that out of the heart come evil thoughts. Hebrews 4:12 says the word of God discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Revelation 10:9-10 shows John eating the scroll, as Jeremiah ate the words. Proverbs 4:23 says to guard your heart.
application:
Ask God to search your heart and show you what you cannot see (Jeremiah 17:10).

Consider where you are trusting in “flesh” this week. Redirect your trust to the LORD.

Receive the word of God as food. Spend time today with a short passage and “eat” it slowly.
prayerPrompts: Confess that your heart is deceitful, and ask him to search it.
Ask him to lead you in the way everlasting.
Thank him that he tests the mind.
